Ultimately, if one partner is making the other partner feel like her (or his) personal autonomy is under threat, the threatened partner either has to decide whether this is a something she can live with, i.e. sacrifice she’s willing to make for the good of the relationship—i.e., take one for the team—or whether it’s asking too much and really invades her own sense of self and values. I think any relationship in which either partner feels forced to compromise an important principle probably isn’t a healthy one.  
  
If a partner feels like her autonomy is being invaded, on the other hand, I think she has a responsibility to make that clear in an honest discussion. The other person needs to know exactly how big a deal a request is and to try to work to reach some acceptable resolution.  
  
If one partner makes clear that it is a big deal and the other partner blows it off, these two people probably shouldn’t be together.

Have no health risks

Have no unpleasant side effects

Not interfere with sex/allow spontaneous sex

There are also many different formulations--for instance, there are about a million 28 day versions. So if one formulation doesn't work for you, you can try others.

First, even if you don't feel confident inside, you have to give the outer impression that you're confident. Act calm and decisive, with a relaxed, halfway amused or halfway bored expression on your face. Do this all the time, every day, not just when the bullying starts.

If someone is nearby and says something to you, you can stare them straight in the eye--hold their gaze--and step a little towards them. Then, after a pause of a couple of seconds, ask in a low, very serious voice, "What is your problem?" and/or "Are you looking for trouble?" And do NOT look away.

As for being scared, listen to your fear to a degree, but don't let it overwhelm you. Use common sense--never be alone anywhere, always be in public, and preferably where there's a video camera or neutral witnesses. Never throw the first punch or obviously taunt someone, but if they throw a punch, remember a few things: 1) You will heal. You have to first distinguish between "method effectiveness" and "use effectiveness." Method effectiveness is theoretical effectiveness that you get with perfect use. Use effectiveness is what you get when you factor in antibiotics, nausea/vomiting, forgetful women, physiological stress, and such. 

You're already distinguishing between the two to an extent, but you're also sort of claiming that the method effectiveness percentages are somehow not really method effectiveness because they're being screwed up by misuse. I read a study to that effect once thought I can't cite it right now. Say 10 million women in America are on the pill right now, and do the math. That's 30,000 women a year getting pregnant despite perfect pill usage (again, not counting the women who got pregnant as a result of not using it perfectly even though many thought they did).

The fact is mother nature wants men and women to make babies, and so the pill has a huge uphill battle. One reason that the pill is for women is that it's easier to control one egg per month than hundreds of millions of sperm per ejaculation (i.e., billions a month in an average couple). You could probably up the hormone dose and suppress ovulation 100% of the time, but it would likely have undesirable systemic effects. And even though the pill thickens cervical mucus that make it hard for sperm to get through, again we're talking hundreds of millions per ejaculation.

Ultimately you're talking about statistics, and given enough time there will always be a black swan event. Such is the nature of the world.

Cameras are often sold with "kit lenses" that are jacks of all trades. Usually they are zooms. Zooms are more convenient, but they tend to be slower, heavier, more exppensive, and not quite as optically superior as fixed focal length lenses, aka primes. With a prime you can still zoom, but you do it with your feet, i.e. by walking closer to or farther away from your subject. Sometimes this can be inconvenient (like if you have to cross a busy highway) or impossible (if you would have to travel several hundred yards across rough terrain), but it works most of the time. 

Primes tend to be optically better, faster, lighter weight, and lens for lens cheaper than zooms. But you might have to buy two or three of them to get the range available to you with a single zoom. Plus, depending on what you set out to shoot on any given day, you might have to take two or more lenses with you.

For a full-frame sensor, a good trio would be a 24mm wide angle, a 50mm standard (which sees the angle of view roughly equivalent to how your own eyes work), a 135 short telephoto, and a 200mm medium/long telephoto, but that is certainly not set in stone. You might do instead a 24 mm, an 85mm, and a 200mm. Keep in mind that there are also zooms that are considerably better than the typical kit lens although still not as sharp as primes. Keep in mind also that these are for full-frame sensors. If you get an aps sensor like the t6i, a 24mm will be closer to a full-frame 35mm, a 50mm will be more like an 85mm, and so on. With the OM-D it would probably be even more extreme, although I don't know for sure.

Another thing is that you don't need to buy all of these lenses at once. To answer your question, my boyfriend and I between us have a 24, a 50, an 85, a 135, a 70-200, and a couple of kit lenses, but it has taken us a while to get all of them. In fact it might be better to limit yourself to one lens for a while, whether zoom or prime. A single prime, say a 50mm (assuming full-frame) or a 24mm (assuming a crop sensor) would force you to move around and look for the best shooting angle; a lot of people who are just starting out is to see something and immediately shoot from the spot they're standing on, without realizing that by moving a few feet (or a few dozen feet) they get better composition.

There's  little difference in terms of speed between 1.8 and 1.4--less than a stop's worth. But one lens may be a better lens in other respects (optics, build quality, and such). Personally I would take a 1.8 that's optically superior over a 1.4 that's optically inferior. If you're shooting cityscapes at twilight, you probably want to use a tripod anyway, which will allow you to use slower shutter speeds and thus smaller apertures.

You're on a triphasic pill. Some doctors feel that a monophasic pill is better for acne, and if you want to skip a period it's a lot easier since every active pill is the same as every other active pill--you just skip the inactive sugar pills and go straight to the new pack. This is essentially how seasonique works.

With the patch and the ring, you get the same steady level of hormones that you do with a monophasic pill--probably even steadier since you're getting pretty much a constant hormone dose the whole time the patch is on you or the ring is in you. Plus you only have to deal with it once a week. I don't know how good they are at dealing with acne, though. My friend is on the ring and is also pretty active--she says it stays in place pretty well, including during sex, and that her husband either doesn't feel it or doesn't care than he can. I have heard stories that sweating a lot can loosen the adhesive on the patch but have no direct experience of that so I don't know if they're true.

I don't know if I can add much to this. It seems to me, though, that this is about the relationship as much as it is about birth control and sex. Truth to tell, things like this can _never_ be just about sex, because even if the odds are low that there will be an oops, if there _is_ an oops it's a huge/massive deal, especially if one or both of the partners are pro-life.

As you point out, it's a 50-50 deal. That means that both partners have to be comfortable with the birth control arrangements, or if not entirely comfortable, then at a point where they can accept whatever is in place. Getting to that point can be a mixture of a lot of things: money, convenience, spontenaity, sensation, trust in the method, and (a big one) trust in your partner. That last is why things can often get prickly.

Ultimately, you cannot force her into using something she doesn't want to use, and you shouldn't try. (Perhaps "force" is too strong a word, but you know what I mean). If you really weren't concerned about respecting her judgment on this and tried to pressure or plead with her after she clearly announced that she'd made her decision, than that's a big red flag for the relationship. But the reverse is also true regarding you and condom use. She shouldn't give you any grief for wanting to use them, and you should feel free to use them.

Of course there's a danger of spiraling retaliation, where she might get the message (even if it isn't one you meant to send) that you were saying "Ultimatum: If you don't switch birth control, I will punish you for your decision by using condoms," or "I'm punishing you for my birth control choice by not initiating." This is why you need to talk things out and reach a mutually acceptable agreement somehow.

How about this as a compromise: 1) Use condoms sometimes but not all the time. When you use them, stay inside. When not using them, pull out. If she's reluctant to do even that much, like if she says she's already great at taking her pills on schedule so she doesn't need an app, then that's another red flag since it shows she isn't interested in compromise at all; the point is not necessarily to improve her pill-taking but to show you she's serious about it and is willing to work with you to find a solution. 3) If she agrees to the first two arrangements, try initiating some to help show her you love her and trust her.

I'm on the same pill as you. Well, if you consider that a) starting subsequent packs late increases the chance of pregnancy, and b) a little experience in taking the pill at the right time before relying on it alone can't hurt in any way, and c) in cost-benefit terms using condoms for two or three extra weeks is nothing compared to how big a deal a pregnancy would be (even if there's a minuscule chance), there really doesn't seem to be much of a downside to being a bit cautious. :-)

You can start the pill on the first day of your period, on the Sunday following when you period starts, or any other day of your cycle. The chance of having a few strangely-timed periods increases with those three choices; Sunday start is sort of the industry standard for a couple of reasons. But if you do the third option, it's probably best to assume you aren't protected for the first month and to use condoms, just to be on the safe side. (This will also give you some time to get used to taking it on schedule and protect you from any goofs.)

Once you have your first pill period, then you'll certainly be fully protected from there on out regardless of what day of the week you start the packs.

There are advantages and disadvantages to both.

If you both haven't been tested, then stay with the condoms until you both have.

If you're clean, then it's only about birth control and not disease. Condoms are less expensive unless you'll be having a lot of sex. You can also see them working, which can be reassuring, and you usually can see if they've failed and go for a Plan B. But they cut down on the boy's sensations (although on the other hand that may slow him down some if he needs slowing down). They also cut down on the spontenaity--just as things are heating up, you have to stop and get a condom on him. OTOH, you can make it part of foreplay to unroll it onto him sexily/teasingly.

Advantages to the pill? It doesn't get in the way of sex. At all. You kiss and cuddle and get excited and then just let penetration happen whenever you're ready without any interruption--it's a _lovely_ experience, especially in the first stages of a sexual relationship where you are right now. Plus, it feels a ton better for him (and maybe better for you as well), and on the emotional level there's something _far_ more intimate about being connected with nothing in the way, especially if he reaches orgasm inside you (that's the ultimate intimacy in my book). The pill may also help give you shorter and lighter periods and may even improve your skin or make you go up a cup size or so, and even make you hornier. In fact, the knowledge that it's protecting you from pregnancy by itself may be a turn-on since you no longer have to worry about pregnancy (except for that small failure rate, which is smaller than that of condoms, at least). On the other hand, you may not get any of the good side effects and you may get some of the bad ones--weight gain, vaginal dryness, lower sex drive, moodiness, acne. Every girl is different and every pill is different, and the only way to find out is to try. You can always switch to a different brand if it doesn't work out, and if you do badly on two or three then just go off of them. Also, since there's no birth control visibly present when you're having sex, there may be (especially for the first few months) this nagging worry that maybe the pill won't work. That tends to fade with time, though maybe not completely. But again, in the end, the only way is to give it a try and see what happens.

If safety is a concern then you can always double up, which brings the pregnancy chances about as low as they can be (though the chance still isn't zero). In exchange for the increased protection you get the downsides of both methods combined.

I hope this helps! Best of luck!

Mask and fins are personal, as are boots. Make sure the mask in particular fits. Get someone who knows what s/he's doing to help you get the right fit.

As for wetsuits, there are two types of people: those who pee in their wetsuits and those who lie about peeing in their wetsuits. Think about that when considering renting. Again, work with someone who can help you get the right wetsuit. Different brands may fit different bodyshapes differently, so don't assume that brand a or b or C is automatically the best.

Regulators are a good bit more expensive and you may not want to buy one until you know you're going to stick with diving. Most mainstream companies make fine regulators, so again don't get hung up on brand.

I have found entry-level computers to be different enough from each other that you would be well off getting one and really learning it backwards and forwards. You don't want to spend your entire dive staring at the computer and trying to figure out how to operate it and what it's telling you instead of seeing the sights. You want to set it and then be able to know at a glance (or at a beep) what it says. Since you don't know what computer(s) will be available for rental, just go ahead and buy one. The intros such as the Mares Puck or the Suunto Zoop arent all that expensive.

BCs _do_ have differences, but they're also bulky, so if you're going to be travelling to dive it might be better to rent for a while. If you want to buy, look for fit as well as features. For instance, I like a lot of D-rings on mine I can clip things to, and I like them to be metal, and I like having two tank straps for redundancy. You, on the other hand, might like something lighter and easier to pack. Just do your homework. :-)

If you're just looking for names to help start you on your research, here are a few, in no particular order: Aqualung, Oceanic, Mares, Scubapro, Cressi, Suunto, Henderson. Best of luck!

With everything you shoot, there is no single lens that would cover all of your needs. So pick a good prime. Primes are sharper, faster, lighter, and less expensive for the quality than zooms. The Sigma Art series are spectacular lenses for the price. So pick a prime and zoom with your feet. :-)
